name: Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga)
overview: The Fulani Walarbe of Gashiga, the majority in their area, live alongside the Fali and the Bata. Coming from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger via Bashéo, Demsa and the Mandara Mountains, they form a hereditary lamidat where Islam governs social life; livestock rearing, farming, trade and Koranic teaching are its pillars.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, integrated with the Fali and the Bata, who largely speak Fulfulde.
Fulfulde is the major language of the North, the Far North and Adamawa.
One may marry into any other ethnic group, provided the religion is the same; formerly, people married only within the group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The lands were acquired gradually, through neighbourliness and marriage alliances.
Origin: Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger; stages in Cameroon at Bashéo, Demsa and in the Mandara Mountains. Ties with these places are maintained.
The mosque is the great place of prayer.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A lamido, whose throne is passed on by inheritance, leads the group; an alkali (judge) dispenses justice at the lamidat.
Men and women live separately; the man provides for the woman's needs, and she does not go out without permission.
Women do not look men in the eye. Relations with neighbours are not always harmonious.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the suitor's family goes to the young girl's family.
Marriages between cousins are permitted.
Steps: request (kola nut and salt), engagement (suitcase given to the fiancée), bride price in money, celebration (suitcase of clothes).
Kola, salt and sweets handed out announce that the girl is promised: those who receive them become witnesses to the engagement.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship: religious life is Islamic.
Symbolic places: Mount Tenguelin, refuge of the Fali during the jihad, and the villages of Pomla Petel, Chakare (“the middle”) and Pomla Manga.
Birth is a blessing that perpetuates the parent; death is the return to God, and people pray for the rest of the deceased.
Taboos: for men, alcohol, gambling, crime; for women, disrespect towards their husband and going out without permission; for children, theft and disrespect towards elders.
Serious offences: crime, adultery, alcohol, hypocrisy, dishonouring one's parents, severely punished.
Mediums predict the future, although this is frowned upon.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: livestock rearing (cattle, sheep, goats) for sale, crops, trade, Quranic teaching. Women: embroidery and beadwork crafts, Quranic teaching.
The land, at first belonging to no one, was appropriated by the monarchy and belongs to the lamidat.
Crafts: cotton weaving, embroidery of boubous, basketry, leatherwork (shoes, clothing, mats, djangardé cloth).

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Boubous for men, wrappers for women.
Traditional medicine is trusted more, being judged faster and longer-lasting.
Beauty: the man of good morals and fine bearing; the refined, slim, well-groomed woman with beautiful hair.
Courtship: the man presentable, well brought up and well off; the woman beautiful, healthy and of good character.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: wadou'el, sorol, dat'do, dogoulayel; instruments: tam-tam, horns, griots' songs.
People dance during Ramadan, Tabaski and the lamido's festival, which brings all the ethnic groups together in front of the palace.

sections.title: The names
items: No particular name structure; the name does not change.
Appellatives: walarbé, djasi, batoudi, bouré.

lessons.title: Who are the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, integrated with the Fali and the Bata, who widely speak Fulfulde. • Fulfulde is the great language of the North, the Far North and Adamawa. • One may marry anyone of another ethnic group, provided the religion is the same; formerly, people married only within the group. • The lands were acquired gradually, through neighbourliness and marriage alliances. • Origin: Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger; Cameroonian stages at Bashéo, Demsa and in the Mandara mountains. Ties with these places are maintained.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Fulani Walarbe of Gashiga, the majority in their area, live alongside the Fali and the Bata. Coming from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger via Bashéo, Demsa and the Mandara Mountains, they form a hereditary lamidat where Islam governs social life; livestock rearing, farming, trade and Koranic teaching are its pillars.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: livestock (cattle, sheep, goats) for sale, farming, trade, Quranic teaching. Women: embroidery and bead crafts, Quranic teaching. • The land, at first belonging to no one, was appropriated by the monarchy and belongs to the lamidat. • Crafts: cotton weaving, embroidery of boubous, basketry, leatherwork (shoes, clothing, mats, djangardé cloth).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: livestock rearing (cattle, sheep, goats) for sale, farming, trade, Koranic teaching. Women: embroidery and beadwork crafts, Koranic teaching. Land, at first owned by no one, was appropriated by the monarchy and belongs to the lamidat.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • No ancestor cult: religious life is Islamic. • Symbolic places: Mount Tenguelin, refuge of the Fali during the jihad, and the villages of Pomla Petel, Chakare (“the middle”) and Pomla Manga. • Birth is a blessing that perpetuates the parent; death is the return to God, and prayers are said for the rest of the deceased. • Prohibitions: for the man, alcohol, games of chance, crime; for the woman, disrespect towards her husband and going out without permission; for the child, theft and disrespect towards elders. • Serious offences: crime, adultery, alcohol, hypocrisy, dishonouring one's parents, severely punished.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor cult: religious life is Islamic. Symbolic places: Mount Tenguelin, refuge of the Fali during the jihad, and the villages of Pomla Petel, Chakare (“the middle”) and Pomla Manga.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Fulfulde
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Fulfulde. • Greeting formulas: Mi hofni = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); A wali djamna = morning greeting (one person); One wali djamna = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Gotel, Didi, Tati, Naye, Djaye. • Appellatives: walarbé, djasi, batoudi, bouré.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Fulfulde are the first steps towards communicating with the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Fulfulde.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Fulfulde are the first steps towards communicating with the Peuls Walarbe (Gashiga). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
